REQUEST  FOR  INFORMATION  (RFI)    for    Utility  Invoice  Audits     Electricity,  Natural  Gas,  &  Water    
 
 
 
 
 
 
Office  of  Facilities  Management  (OFM)    Public  Building  Services  (PBS)    US  General  Services  Administration  (GSA)     

  
A.  Description    The  U.S.  General  Services  Administration  (GSA),  on  behalf  of  the  Office  of  Facilities  
Management
 
(OFM),
 
is
 
requesting
 
information
 
from
 
contractors
 
interested
 
in
 
and
 
capable
 
of
 
providing
 
utility
 
invoice
 
audit
 
support.
 
This
 
support
 
includes
 
auditing
 
invoices
 
for
 
electricity
 
(NAICS
 
221122),
 
natural
 
gas
 
(NAICS
 
221210),
 
and
 
water
 
(NAICS
 
221300).
    THIS  IS  A  REQUEST  FOR  INFORMATION  (RFI)  ONLY .  This  Request  for  Information  
(RFI)
 
is
 
issued
 
strictly
 
for
 
planning
 
purposes
 
and
 
to
 
gather
 
information;
 
it
 
is
 
not
 
a
 
Request
 
for
 
Quote
 
(RFQ)
 
and
 
should
 
not
 
be
 
construed
 
as
 
a
 
commitment
 
to
 
issue
 
an
 
RFQ
 
in
 
the
 
future.
 
The
 
GSA
 
is
 
not
 
seeking
 
quotes
 
at
 
this
 
time
 
and
 
will
 
not
 
accept
 
unsolicited
 
quotes.
  GSA  is  not  obligated  to  contract  for  any  supply  or  service  based  on  this  RFI.  The  U.S.  Government  
will
 
not
 
reimburse
 
respondents
 
for
 
any
 
costs
 
associated
 
with
 
preparing
 
or
 
submitting
 
a
 
response;
 
all
 
such
 
costs
 
are
 
the
 
sole
 
responsibility
 
of
 
the
 
interested
 
party.
  A  decision  not  to  respond  to  this  RFI  will  not  disqualify  a  party  from  participating  in  any  potential  
future
 
RFQ.
 
 
B.  Background    The  U.S.  General  Services  Administration  (GSA)  manages  utility  services  for  its  own  federal  
facilities
 
and
 
those
 
of
 
other
 
Federal
 
Agencies.
 
This
 
involves
 
procuring
 
substantial
 
amounts
 
of
 
energy
 
annually:
 
approximately
 
4.4
 
million
 
megawatt-hours
 
(MWh)
 
of
 
electricity
 
and
 
20.2
 
million
 
dekatherms
 
(Dths)
 
of
 
natural
 
gas.
 
These
 
services
 
are
 
provided
 
across
 
300+
 
accounts
 
for
 
over
 
26
 
different
 
U.S.
 
Federal
 
Agencies.
 
Given  this  scale,  it  is  crucial  for  the  U.S.  Government  to  ensure:  
●  Accurate  billing  from  all  natural  gas  and  electricity  suppliers/utilities.  ●  Invoice  compliance  with  all  contractual  obligations  and  federal  regulations.  ●  Effective  tracking  of  utility  service  costs,  financial  data,  and  any  detected  invoice  
discrepancies.
 
C.  RFI  Objective    The  Government  will  utilize  information  from  this  RFI  to  identify  the  number  of  companies  that   can  
potentially
 
meet
 
the
 
Government’s
 
scope,
 
as
 
described
 
below.
 
 
Utility  Invoice  Audit  Requirements  
The  vendor  shall  perform  the  following  core  services:  
●  Audit  and  Correct  Invoices:  Review  utility  bills  (electricity,  natural  gas,  and  water)  to  ensure  
accuracy.
 
If
 
errors
 
are
 
identified,
 
the
 
vendor
 
must
 
obtain
 
bill
 
credits
 
or
 
recovered
 
monies
 
from
 
the
 
utility/energy
 
supplier
 
on
 
behalf
 
of
 
the
 
Federal
 
agency.
 ●  Maintain  Comprehensive  Records:  Maintain  a  readily  accessible  electronic  record  (Excel  and/or  
PDF
 
format)
 
for
 
all
 
agencies
 
covered
 
under
 
the
 
contract.
 
This
 
record
 
must
 
include:
 

○  Updates  on  billing  disputes.  ○  Budget  figures  related  to  agency  accounts.  ○  Relevant  historical  usage  data.  ○  Note:  The  vendor  may  use  their  own  system  of  record,  provided  reports  can  be  furnished  promptly  upon  Government  request.  ●  Provide  Reporting:  Deliver  reports  on  the  status  of  ongoing  contract  work  to  GSA  and  participating  Agencies  on  at  least  a  quarterly  basis .    
GSA  anticipates  this  contract  may  be:    ●  Single-Award,  Indefinite  Delivery/Indefinite  Quantity  (IDIQ,  Firm  Fixed  Price  (FFP)  Contract    ●  FFP  Task  Order  will  be  issued  against  the  IDIQ    ●  Base  year  and  several  option  years.    ●  NAICS  Code:  541690 ,  Other  Scientific  and  Technical  Consulting  Services  
This  approach  may  enable  Federal  Agencies  to  place  orders  for  bill  auditing  and  cost  recovery   services,  and  aligns  with  GSA’s  broader  strategic  goals  to  maximize  government-wide  cost   savings .   
D.  RFI  Responses    For  consistent  and  easy  review,  please  ensure  responses,  excluding  the  cover  page  and  any  attachments,  do  not  exceed  10  pages .  All  interested  parties  must  submit  the  following  minimum  information:   1.  Name  of  Company    2.  Company  Website    3.  Company  POC,  Telephone  Number,  &  Email  Address    4.  Company  Address    5.  SAM  Unique  Entity  ID    6.  Business  Designation  -  Small  or  Large  7.  GSA  contract  number(s)  -  if  applicable  -  and  Company’s  socioeconomic  status    8.  Company  capabilities  as  they  relate  to  services  described  in  this  notice.  This  will  help   confirm  if  Vendors  can  meet  the  demands  of  a  national  contract,  assess  Vendor   readiness,  pricing  flexibility,  and  support  for  broader  federal  participation:    
a.  National  Capacity  &  Scalability    ●  Describe  ability  to  provide  utility  bill  auditing  services  for  locations  across   the  U.S.    ●  What  experience  do  you  have  supporting  federal  clients  on  a  national   scale  for  any  services?    ●  Describe  any  teaming  /  subcontracting  your  Company  anticipates  utilizing   in  support  of  these  requirements.    ●  Provide  the  staffing  footprint,  including  number  of  locations,  quantity,  and   how  /  where  that  quantity  is  distributed  nationally.    
b.  Past  Performance  &  Innovation  

●  Share  examples  of  measurable  cost  recoveries  from  similar  contracts.  ●  What  innovations  or  tools  differentiate  your  audit  methodology?  ●  Describe  the  auditing  standards  and  compliance  protocols  followed  by  your  Company.    c.  Pricing  Structure    ●  Describe  your  pricing  typically  structured  (e.g.,  fixed  fee,  performance  based,  percentage  of  recovered  savings)?  The  Government  prefers  a  fixed  fee  structure,  with  task  options  available  at  additional  cost.    ●  How  would  pricing  be  impacted  if  the  scope  included  nationwide  coverage   or  multiple  agency  participation?    
d.  Multi-Agency  Support    ●  How  would  your  Company  manage  concurrent  task  orders  issued  by   multiple  agencies?    e.  Tools  &  Reporting    ●  Do  you  offer  client  dashboards  or  audit  tracking  platforms?    ●  How  would  your  Company  track  utility  bill  issues  /  recoveries?   
9.  Other  relevant  information  that  is  not  listed  above  which  the  Government  should   consider  in  finalizing  its  market  research  and  acquisition  strategy.    
E.  RFI  Submission  Deadline    Interested  companies  should  submit  responses  through  email  by  3:00PM  Eastern  Time,   Monday,  May  4th  2026 .  Responses  should  be  submitted  as  follows:    
●  Addressed  To:   ○  Sharon  McCreary   Contracting  Officer    sharon.mccreary@gsa.gov   
●  Subject  Line :  RFI  Response  -  Utility  Invoice  Audit  (Company  Name)    
●  Format:  Please  submit  your  response  as  a  single,  comprehensive  PDF  document.  The  organization  of  the  PDF  should  mirror  the  structure  of  the  RFI  Response  Section  detailed  previously.

FOR

1.0. General 
1.1. The contractor shall provide all personnel, equipment, supplies, tools, materials, supervision, and 
other items as required to perform maintenance, testing, monitoring, documentation, emergency service, 
and repairs for the MTC’s UPS as defined in this PWS. 
1.2. Background: Uninterruptible Power Systems (UPS) are critical components of our infrastructure, 
ensuring continuous and reliable power to essential systems and equipment.  The primary function of a 
UPS is to provide instantaneous backup power in the event of a primary power source failure, preventing 
data loss, operational disruptions, and equipment damage.  This service is critical to extending the 
operational lifespan of the UPS equipment as well as maintaining the operational readiness of our most 
vital electrical systems. To ensure the consistent and effective operation of these systems, a robust 
maintenance and repair program is necessary to minimize the downtime and operational disruptions.  
1.3. Period of Performance (PoP). The PoP shall be 15 March 2026 -14 March 2031, 60 months. 
1.4. General Information: 
1.4.1. Place and Performance of Services: Building 5-4 at Fort Indiantown Gap, Annville PA 17003. A 
map identifying the exact location will be provided as an exhibit to this PWS.  
1.4.1.1. Telework: The Government will not permit the contractor to telework in support of this 
requirement. In furtherance of Continuity of Operations Planning (COOP), a telework program may 
be enacted to ensure that the Government's mission -critical operations stay operational during times 
of national emergency or incidents of national significance. Telework shall be at no additional cost 
to the Government. 
1.4.1.2. Unscheduled gate closures by the Fort Indiantown Gap OPS Security may occur at any time 
causing all personnel entering or exiting a closed installation to experience a delay. This cannot be 
predicted or prevented. Contractors are not compensated for unexpected closures or delays. Vehicles 
operated by contractor personnel are subject to search pursuant to applicable regulations. Any moving 
violation of any applicable motor vehicle regulation may result in the termination of the contractor 
employee’s installation driving privileges. 
1.4.1.3. The contractor’s employees shall become familiar with and obey the regulations of the 
installation, including fire, traffic, safety and security regulations while on the installation. Contractor 
employees should only enter restricted areas when required to do so and only upon prior approval. All 
contract employees shall carry proper identification with them at all times, and shall be subject to such 
checks as may be deemed necessary. The contractor shall ensure compliance with all regulations and 
orders of the installation, which may affect performance.  The Government reserves the right to direct the 
removal of an employee from Government property or revoke access to Government systems for 
misconduct, security reasons, or any overt evidence of communicable disease. Removal of contractor 
employees for reasons stated above does not relieve the Contractor from responsibility for total 
performance of this contract. 
1.4.2. Recognized Holidays: The following are recognized US holidays. The contractor shall perform 
services on these days:   

                                                                                                                       3

1.4.2.2. Martin Luther King, Jr.'s Birthday

applicable installation/facility access and local security policies and procedures which may be 
obtained from the POC. The contractor and all associated subcontractor employees shall 
provide all information required for background checks to meet installation access 
requirements to be accomplished by installation Provost Marshal Office, Director of 
Emergency Services, or Security Office. The contractor shall ensure compliance  with all 
personal identity verification requirements as directed by Department of Defense (DoD), 
Headquarters Department of Army (HQDA) and/or local policy (see PWS 6.0). Should the 
Force Protection Condition (FPCON) change, the Government may require cha nges in 
contractor security matters or processes.  
1.4.5.1. For contractors requiring Common Access Card (CAC): NOT APPLICABLE. For contractors that do 
not require a CAC but require access to a DoD facility or  installation: Contractor and all associated sub -
contractors employees shall comply with PMR 525-2 Annex B, and any applicable installation, facility and 
area commander installation/facility access, and local  security policies and  procedures (provided  by a 
Government representative). 
 
1.4.5.2. Awareness Training (AT) Level 1. All contractor employees, to include subcontractor employees, 
requiring access Army installations, facilities and controlled access areas shall complete AT Level I 
Awareness training within 30 calendar days after contract start date or effective date of incorporation of 
this requirement into the contract, whichever is applicable. The contractor shall submit certificates of 
completion for each affected contractor employee and subcontractor employee, to the COR or to the 
contracting officer, if a COR is not assigned, within 30 calendar days after completion of training by all 
employees and subcontractor personnel. AT level I Awareness training is available at the following 
website: http://jko.jten.mil. 
1.4.5.3. iWATCH Training: The contractor and all associated sub‐contractors shall brief all employees on 
the local iWATCH Army program (training standards provided by the requiring activity ATO). This local 
developed training will be used to inform employees of the types of behavior to watch for and instruct 

                                                                                                                       4 
 
employees to report suspicious activity to the COR. This training shall be completed within 30 calendar 
days of contract award and within 30 calendar days of new employees commencing performance with the 
results reported to the COR NLT 30 calendar days after contract award. Locally developed iWATCH 
training is available at: https://armyeitaas.sharepoint-mil.us/:u:/r/sites/NGPA-G34/SitePages/PA-G34-
iWatch.aspx?csf=1&web=1&e=b9Ze7S  
1.4.5.4.  
1.4.5.5. Communications Security/Information Technology (COMSEC/IT) Security. All 
communications with DoD organizations are subject to COMSEC review. All telephone 
communications networks are continually subject to intercept by unfriendly intelligence 
organizations. DoD has authorized the military departments to conduct COMSEC monitoring and 
recording of telephone calls originating from, or terminating at, DoD organizations. Therefore, the 
contractor is advised that any time contractor personnel place or receive a call they are subject to 
COMSEC procedures. The contractor shall ensure wide and frequent dissemination of the above 
information to all employees dealing with DoD information. The contractor shall abide by all 
Government regulations concerning the authorized use of the Government's computer network, 
including the restriction against using the network to recruit Government personnel or advertise job 
openings.

1.4.6. Physical Security. The contractor shall safeguard all Government property provided  for 
contractor use. At the close of each work period, Government facilities, equipment and 
materials shall be secured. 
1.4.6.1. Key Control. NOT APPLICABLE 
1.4.6.2. Lock Combinations: NOT APPLICABLE

1.4.8. Post Award Conferences/Periodic Progress Meetings: The contractor agrees to  attend any 
post award conference convened by the KO in ac cordance with FAR 42.5. The KO, POC and 
other Government personnel, as appropriate, may meet periodically with the  contractor to review 
the contactor’s performance. At these meetings, the KO will apprise the contractor of how the 
Government views the contractor’s performance, and the contractor shall apprise the Government 

                                                                                                                       5 
 
of problems, if any, being experienced. The contractor shall  resolve outstanding issues raised by 
the Government. Contractor attendance at these  meetings shall be at no additional cost to the 
Government. 
1.4.9. Contract Manager (CM): The contactor shall designate a CM who shall ensure performance 
under this contract. For purposes of this contract, the CM is the Dining Facility Manager (DFM) and 
will be referred to as CM/DFM. The name of this person, and an alternate who shall act for the 
contractor when the CM/DFM is absent, shall be designated in writing to the KO. The CM/DFM or 
alternate shall have full authority to act for the contractor on all contract matters relating to daily 
operation of this contract. The CM/DFM shall work through the POC to resolve issues, receive 
technical instructions, and ensure adequate performance of services. The CM/DFM shall ensure that 
contractor employees do not perform any services outside the scope of the contract without an official 
modification issued by the KO. The CM/DFM shall ensure contractor employees understand that 
services performed outside the scope of the contract are performed wholly at the expense of the 
contractor. 
1.4.10. Identification of Contractor Employees: All contractor personnel attending meetings,  
answering Government telephones and working in other situations where their contractor  status 
is not obvious to third parties are required to identify themselves as such to avoid  creating an 
impression that they are Government employees. The contractor shall ensure  that all documents 
or reports produced by contractor personnel are suitably marked as  contractor products or that 
contractor participation is appropriately disclosed.  The contractor’s status as a “contractor” shall 
be predominantly displayed in all correspondence types (to include signature blocks on e -mail) 
and dealings with Government or non - Government entities. Contractor personnel shall wear 
identification badges distinguishing  themselves as such. The badges shall have the company 
name, employee name and the word “contractor” displayed. 
1.4.10.1. The contractor shall retrieve all identification media (including vehicle passes) from its  
employees who depart employment for any reason. The contractor shall return all identification media 
(i.e., badges and vehicles passes) to the KO within 14 days of an employee’s departure. 
1.4.11. Combating Trafficking in Persons: The United States Government has adopted a zero-
tolerance policy regarding trafficking in persons. Contractors and contractor employees shall not 
engage in severe forms of trafficking in persons during the period of performance of the contract; 
procure commercial sex acts during the period of performance of the contract; or use forced labor in 
the performance of the contract. The Contractor shall notify its employees of the United States 
Government’s zero tolerance policy, the actions that will be taken against employees for violations of 
this policy. The contractor shall take appropriate action, up to and including termination, against 
employees or subcontractors that violate the US Government policy as described at FAR 22.17. 
1.4.12. Contractor Travel: NOT APPLICABLE. 
1.4.13. Data Rights: NOT APPLICABLE 
1.4.14. Organizational Conflicts of Interest: Organizational Conflicts of Interest (OCI): The  
contractor and subcontractor personnel performing services under this contract may  receive, have 
access to or participate in the development of proprietary or source selection  information (e.g., 
cost or pricing information, budget information or analyses, specifications  or work statements, 
etc.) or perform evaluation services which may create a current or  subsequent OCls, as defined in 
FAR Subpart 9.5. The contractor shall  notify the POC immediately whenever it becomes aware that 
such access or participation may result in any actual or potential OCI and shall promptly submit a

determined to be acceptable solely at the  discretion of the POC and in the event the POC 
unilaterally determines that any such OCI  cannot be satisfactorily avoided or mitigated, the POC 
may affect other remedies as he or  she deems necessary, including prohibiting the contractor 
from participation in subsequent  contracted requirements which may  be affected by the OCI.

PERFORMANCE WORK STATEMENT 
FOR 
Transportation Command (TRANSCOM) Reference Data Management (TRDM) 
In Support of the United States Transportation Command 
 
Contract Number: TBD 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
DATE: TBD 
 
Prepared by 
UNITED STATES TRANSPORTATION COMMAND 
DIRECTORATE OF COMMAND, CONTROL, COMMUNICATIONS AND CYBER 
SYSTEMS 
 


 
 
Table of Contents 
1. Background ............................................................................................................................... 3 
2. Scope ......................................................................................................................................... 3 
3. Goal ........................................................................................................................................... 3 
4. Brief Summary of the Task Areas ............................................................................................... 3 
5. Brief Summary of the "Shall" Statements .................................................................................. 4 
6. Brief Summary of the Deliverables ............................................................................................. 5 
7. Period of Performance ............................................................................................................... 5 
8. Brief Summary of the DoD Cyber Workforce Framework (DCWF) Code Assignments ............... 5 
 
 
 
 
  

1. Background 
The United States Transportation Command (USTRANSCOM) is a combatant command that 
provides global transportation and logistics support. The TRANSCOM Reference Data 
Management (TRDM) system is the official Program of Record for the command's enterprise 
reference data. TRDM's mission is to collect, maintain, and distribute standardized reference data 
from authoritative sources to ensure data interoperability and synchronization across all 
USTRANSCOM systems and partners. 
2. Scope 
The scope of this project is to provide the technical operation, maintenance, and distribution of 
the TRDM system and its data. The contractor will be responsible for a wide range of support 
tasks, including but not limited to: 
• Requirement analysis 
• Data collection and management 
• Interface and architecture validation 
• Data distribution 
• Implementation, planning, and documentation related to the software development 
lifecycle 
3. Goal 
The primary goal is to establish and maintain TRDM as a trusted and authoritative source of 
reference data for the entire USTRANSCOM enterprise, its users, and its interconnection 
partners. The program prioritizes adherence to key initiatives such as Data Governance, Data 
Security, Modernization, and Zero Trust. 
4. Brief Summary of the Task Areas 
The contractor is responsible for comprehensive management and support across five main areas: 
• Contract Management: Includes overall program management, regular reporting (weekly, 
monthly), progress reviews, security reviews, and managing the transition-in and 
transition-out processes. 
• User Access & Operations Support: Involves maintaining the TRDM websites on both 
unclassified and classified networks (AWS GovCloud), managing user access, providing 
help desk support during business hours (0800-1800 CT), and ensuring data access 
complies with DoD security policies. 
• System Service Management: Encompasses the management of incidents, system 
configuration, changes, software releases, and knowledge. This includes facilitating the 

Configuration Control Board (CCB), managing data change requests, and maintaining 
interconnection agreements. 
• System Operations Management: Focuses on the technical health and security of the 
system. Responsibilities include monitoring system resources, automating data exchange 
through web services, managing capacity and load balancing, executing the vulnerability 
management (IA VM) program, and performing database administration (PostgreSQL), 
backup, and recovery. 
• Data Management and Sharing: Requires advanced data engineering to build and 
maintain data pipelines (ETL/ELT), manage data quality, maintain the data catalog and 
metadata, oversee the data lifecycle, and document the data architecture. 
• Cybersecurity: Requires  comprehensive cybersecurity obligations for government 
contractors, detailing requirements for incident reporting, secure software development, 
workforce qualifications, and adherence to the Risk Management Framework (RMF). 
5. Brief Summary of the "Shall" Statements 
The PWS contains numerous mandatory requirements ("shall" statements). The most critical 
obligations related to security and compliance are summarized below: 
• Personnel Security: All contractor personnel shall be U.S. citizens and shall possess a 
minimum of a final Secret security clearance. This clearance shall be maintained for the 
duration of the contract. 
• Cybersecurity Framework and Policies: The contractor shall support all activities to 
obtain and maintain the Risk Management Framework (RMF) Authorization to Operate 
(ATO). The contractor shall also comply with all relevant DoD, USTRANSCOM, and 
Federal cybersecurity policies and shall participate in an Annual Security Review (ASR). 
• Vulnerability and Risk Management: The contractor shall execute the Information 
Assurance Vulnerability Management (IA VM) program, perform static and dynamic code 
scans before deployment, and remediate all "Critical" and "High" findings. A Plan of 
Action & Milestones (POA&M) for all vulnerabilities shall be developed and maintained. 
• Secure Development and Operations: All development shall adhere to secure coding 
practices. The contractor shall enforce role-based access controls and conduct annual 
failover and recovery exercises. 
• Incident Reporting: The contractor shall report all cyber incidents to the government 
within 72 hours of discovery and shall deliver a detailed Cyber Incident Report within 72 
hours of resolution. 
• General Reporting and Documentation: Beyond security, the contractor shall deliver 
regular reports (Weekly, Monthly), create and maintain management plans 
(Configuration, Backup, Transition), and provide materials and minutes for quarterly 
reviews. 

6. Brief Summary of the Deliverables 
The contractor is required to provide numerous deliverables throughout the contract period. The 
most significant ones include: 
• Regular Reports: Weekly Activities Report (WAR), Monthly Status Report (MSR), and 
Monthly Metrics Report (MMR). 
• Management Plans: A Contract Management Plan at the start of the contract, a 
Transition-In Plan, and a Transition-Out Plan. Several system-level plans (e.g., Failover 
Guide, CM Plan) must be reviewed and updated annually. 
• Reviews and Meetings: Presentation materials and minutes for quarterly In Progress 
Reviews (IPRs) and an Annual Security Review (ASR). 
• Security and RMF Artifacts: A Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) Report, Cyber-
Incident Reports as needed, and all necessary documentation to support the RMF 
Authorization to Operate (ATO). 
• Other Direct Costs (ODC) Purchase Requests: All ODC purchases require the contractor 
to submit a written request with competitive quotes to the COR at least five business days 
in advance. 
7. Period of Performance 
The contract is structured with a one-month transition period, a one-year base period, and four 
one-year option periods. 
• Transition Period: September 1, 2026 – September 30, 2026 
• Base Period: October 1, 2026 – September 30, 2027 
• Option Period One: Through September 30, 2028 
• Option Period Two: Through September 30, 2029 
• Option Period Three: Through September 30, 2030 
• Option Period Four: Through September 30, 2031 
8. Brief Summary of the DoD Cyber Workforce Framework (DCWF) Code Assignments 
The PWS mandates that all personnel performing cyberspace work be qualified according to the 
DCWF. Most positions are designated as IT Privileged Users and require specific certifications. 
• Key Roles Identified: The assigned codes correspond to roles such as Program Manager, 
Systems Administrator, Software Developer, Database Administrator, Systems Security 
Analyst, Information System Security Officer, and Data Architect/Engineer. 
• Required Certifications: The required Computing Environment (CE) certifications are 
primarily focused on Amazon Web Services (AWS), including AWS Certified Cloud 

Practitioner, Developer, Solutions Architect, and Data Engineer. SecurityX, CISM, 
Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), Database certifications for 
PostgreSQL are also required.

Vision Statement 

Ginnie Mae’s vision is to strengthen its Risk and Controls Self-Assessment (RCSA) Program and promote an enterprise-wide holistic view of its operational and information technology risk profile with the comprehensive participation of each Office and Division in the identification, assessment, and mitigation of risk to ensure a risk-informed approach to internal controls that enhances decision-making, improves program performance, and ensures integrity of operations. 


1 General Information

1.1 Scope of Work 

The  successful contractor shall provide program management support for the continued enhancement and execution of the performed across the enterprise. The Risk and Controls Self-Assessment (RCSA) Program identifies, assesses, reports and monitors risks and controls associated with operational processes, people, systems, and external events. Ginnie Mae’s risk management framework and governance structure provides comprehensive control and ongoing management of the major inherent and residual risk associated with its business activities.

The Contractor will review, analyze and assess governance documentation, manuals, and other materials provided by all eight (8) of Ginnie Mae’s Offices, update Process Flow Charts, Risk Register Control Matrices, Narratives for each Office and other RCSA documents on an annual basis. This includes templates, Process and SOP inventories, and other similar documentation.

The support services shall include but not be limited to: 

Project Work Plan

Transition Services

RCSA Annual Maintenance 

Special Projects 

Detailed descriptions of specific tasks are provided in Section 5 Specific Tasks and Deliverables.

1.2 Background 

In the critical role that Ginnie Mae plays in the secondary mortgage market, it faces numerous enterprise-wide operational risks that must be proactively monitored and mitigated. Some risks are consistently present, highly visible, inherent, and broadly understood; others may be recognized at some level but may not be highly visible and fully understood; yet other risks may evolve over time or emerge suddenly. 

RCSA is responsible for assisting Ginnie Mae’s business units to recognize, understand, and establish appropriate strategies to mitigate identified risks. 

Ginnie Mae will be most successful in managing risks if a high level of risk awareness exists within its eight (8) business offices. The RCSA Program supports Divisions within these Offices in defining tolerances for specific risks and considers the cost and benefit of associated internal controls to manage risks. The RCSA Program enables Ginnie Mae to better connect and integrate risk across the organization while seeking to streamline internal controls across the agency to enhance their value to Ginnie Mae’s corporate governance.

Ginnie Mae’s strategic vision for the RCSA program is not just compliance, but also risk culture, risk awareness, risk ownership, and risk advisement through the inclusion of risks as an integral part of day-to-day program management. While the RCSA Program’s primary review focus is operational and information technology risks, it also seeks to monitor current and emerging risks including, but not limited to, credit, governance, legal, reputational, and strategic risks.

The ORAD works in partnership with the Offices and Divisions to implement the RCSA Program through a three-prong review with a five-step iterative methodology to identify, assess, analyze, and remediate known risks, control gaps, potential emerging issues, and other threats as determined during the review.

The Contractor will perform individual assessments and reviews in eight (8) Offices within Ginnie Mae and support ORAD to determine risks, gaps, mitigation strategies and continuous RCSA improvement activities, in addition to its program management duties.

UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
Request for Information (RFI) on Biologically-Derived Materials for Transient Propulsion 
Systems 
Agency: Office of the Director of National Intelligence 
Office: Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity 
RFI Number: IARPA-RFI-26-01 
 
 
Synopsis 
The Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity (IARPA) seeks information regarding the 
current state of the art (SOTA) in biologically-derived materials suitable for controlled transience in 
propulsion systems for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). IARPA is interested in understanding how 
controlled material degradation can be extended beyond structural components to include 
turbines, engines, motors, and associated propulsion elements. Of particular interest are 
approaches that move beyond ultraviolet (UV)-initiated or water (H2O)-initiated transience 
mechanisms and subsequently enable more diverse triggering modalities that are stable in a range 
of environmental conditions.  This RFI is issued for planning purposes only and does not constitute 
a formal solicitation for proposals or suggest the procurement of any materials, components, or 
systems. 
 
Background 
The proliferation of UAV operations across military, intelligence, and civilian domains has raised 
growing concerns about the environmental footprint of aerospace materials, particularly in 
scenarios where systems may be lost. Conventional propulsion components, and their controls, 
fabricated from persistent materials— metal alloys, engineering plastics, and advanced 
composites— can remain in ecosystems for decades or centuries. DARPA's ICARUS (Inbound, 
Controlled, Air-Releasable, Unrecoverable Systems) program pioneered a solution for airframe 
structures by demonstrating transient materials that maintain operational performance before 
undergoing controlled degradation, thereby minimizing persistent environmental residue. The 
ICARUS approach employed primarily UV-triggered photopolymers that undergo programmable 
degradation of structural components, establishing proof-of-concept. However, extending these 
achievements beyond airframes to propulsion systems and their controls reveals critical 
limitations: propulsion components operate under extreme thermal, mechanical, and chemical 
stresses; contain a mixture of material types; must maintain structural integrity throughout 
dynamic mission profiles; require materials compatible with combustion environments or 
electromagnetic fields; and face significant challenges when UV initiation serves as the primary 
degradation trigger within enclosed or shielded propulsion assemblies where UV exposure may be 
limited or absent. Moreover, there may be operational parameters where natural UV exposure is 
present.  Environmental conditions that naturally degrade materials— humidity, microbial activity, 
thermal cycling, oxidation— are often more readily available than UV exposure, suggesting 

UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
opportunities for bio-derived materials that leverage natural decomposition pathways to control 
degradation of an airborne system. 
Biological systems offer compelling templates for addressing these challenges. Nature has evolved 
diverse materials that combine high-performance mechanical properties with controlled 
degradation pathways responsive to environmental triggers including enzymatic activity, pH, 
humidity, thermal cycling, and oxidative conditions. Examples span structural proteins (silk, 
keratin, collagen), polysaccharides (chitin, cellulose), fungal materials, bio-acrylics, and 
biocomposites that demonstrate remarkable strength-to-weight ratios while remaining inherently 
biodegradable under appropriate conditions. 
Biologically derived materials including wood, paper, gums, cottons, and waxes still play a role in 
defense related materials, but recent advances in materials science, synthetic biology, and 
biomanufacturing have expanded the palette of engineered biological materials suitable for 
demanding applications. These include genetically modified structural proteins with tailored 
mechanical properties, bio-derived ceramics and composites for high-temperature applications, 
enzymatically-sensitive polymers with programmable degradation kinetics, and mycelium-based 
materials offering tunable porosity and mechanical performance. Yet significant gaps remain in 
translating these materials from laboratory demonstrations to operational propulsion systems that 
must reliably perform under extreme conditions before undergoing controlled transience. 
 
Scope 
This RFI specifically targets the unique challenges of propulsion systems and their controls, where 
materials must simultaneously satisfy competing requirements of high-performance operation and 
controlled degradation with limited degradation of UAV capability. IARPA seeks to understand 
potential pathways toward propulsion components fabricated from, coated with, or incorporating 
biologically-derived materials that enable: 
1. Operational performance matching or approaching conventional propulsion materials 
during mission lifetime 
2. Controlled transience initiated by environmental triggers beyond UV exposure 
3. Predictable degradation kinetics allowing mission planning around component lifetime 
4. Minimal residue following transience, leaving limited environmental signature 
5. Scalable manufacturing compatible with rapid prototyping and production requirements 
Propulsion Components of Interest 
• Turbine/Engine Elements 
• Electric Motor Components 
• Auxiliary Systems 
 

UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
Questions for Respondents 
IARPA seeks improved understanding across the following areas. Responses addressing one, 
some, or all questions are encouraged: 
Current SOTA Assessment 
1. What biologically-derived materials have demonstrated mechanical, thermal, and 
chemical properties approaching those required for propulsion system components (e.g., 
turbine blades, combustion chambers, motor housings)? 
2. What are the current performance limitations of bio-derived materials in high-temperature 
(>500°C), high-stress (>100 MPa), or chemically-aggressive environments relevant to 
propulsion systems? 
3. What manufacturing approaches can produce bio-derived propulsion components with the 
dimensional tolerances, surface finishes, and quality control required for reliable 
operation? 
4. What examples exist of bio-derived materials demonstrating controlled transience while 
maintaining operational performance? What degradation timescales have been achieved 
(hours, days, weeks)? 
Material Systems and Architectures 
5. What bio-derived material classes (proteins, polysaccharides, fungal materials, 
biocomposites, bio-acrylics, bio-ceramics) show greatest promise for propulsion 
applications? What are their operational temperature, strength, and durability limits? 
6. Can hybrid architectures (bio-derived matrices with conventional reinforcements, or vice 
versa) provide transitional pathways toward fully-transient propulsion systems? 
7. What surface treatments, coatings, or protective layers can enable bio-derived materials to 
withstand propulsion environments while maintaining transience capability? 
8. How can hierarchical material structures inspired by biology (e.g., nacre, bone, wood) be 
engineered to provide both high performance and controlled degradation? 
Transience Mechanisms and Triggers 
9. What non-UV environmental triggers can initiate controlled degradation in bio-derived 
materials suitable for propulsion applications? How can trigger sensitivity be engineered? 
10. How can degradation kinetics be tailored to match mission requirements (e.g., maintain 
integrity through mission duration, then degrade within hours of exposure to trigger)? 
11. What approaches can provide fail-safe mechanisms ensuring transience even if primary 
triggers are not encountered? How can premature degradation be prevented? 
12. Can enzymatic or microbial degradation be engineered to occur predictably across diverse 
environmental conditions? What biological agents enable reliable transience? 

UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
Integration and System Considerations 
13. What propulsion system components represent the most tractable initial targets for bio-
derived transient materials? Which pose the greatest technical challenges? 
14. How do bio-derived propulsion materials affect overall system design (thermal 
management, lubricants, fuel compatibility, electromagnetic properties)? 
15. What testing protocols and performance metrics are needed to validate bio-derived 
propulsion components for UAV applications? How can reliability be assessed? 
16. What manufacturing scale-up challenges exist for bio-derived propulsion materials? What 
production timelines and costs are realistic? 
Research Gaps and Opportunities 
17. What fundamental research advances are needed to enable bio-derived transient 
propulsion systems? What are the highest-risk, highest-payoff research directions? 
18. Where can synthetic biology, genetic engineering, or directed evolution accelerate 
development of materials tailored for transient propulsion applications? 
19. What adjacent fields (biomineralization, structural biology, biomaterials, 
biomanufacturing) offer underutilized approaches applicable to this challenge? 
20. What performance trade-offs are inherent in bio-derived transient materials, and how might 
mission concepts adapt to exploit their unique properties? 
 
Preparation Instructions to Respondents 
IARPA requests that respondents submit focused responses addressing one or more of the 
questions above. Submissions should include a brief technical description of relevant approaches, 
materials, or concepts; outline critical technical obstacles and potential pathways to address 
them; and comment on expected performance, limitations, and development timelines. Where 
appropriate, respondents may provide a non-proprietary rough order of magnitude (ROM) estimate 
of funding and resources required for research programs spanning one to four years. This 
announcement contains all information required to submit a response. No additional forms, kits, 
or other materials are needed. 
IARPA welcomes responses from all capable and qualified sources including academia, industry, 
government laboratories, and federally funded research entities from within and outside the U.S. In 
response to submissions, IARPA may organize an invitation-only workshop for reviewing and 
discussing relevant research. Participants may be asked to make presentations based on their RFI 
submissions or associated research. Written submissions and workshop discussions may inform 
formulation of future U.S. Government research initiatives. 
Formatting Requirements 
Responses must meet the following specifications: 

UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
1. Cover sheet (one page) identifying the title, organization(s), and technical/administrative 
points of contact— including names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses of 
all co-authors— and clearly indicating association with IARPA-RFI-26-01. 
2. Executive summary (one-half page maximum) providing a substantive, focused overview; 
3. Technical response (maximum three pages) addressing one, some, or all questions posed 
above; 
4. Detailed technical description (maximum two pages) of technical challenges and 
potential research approaches relevant to biologically-derived transient propulsion 
materials; 
o A single quad-chart (PowerPoint slide or PDF) depicting the approach, key 
concepts, supportive illustrations, and potential impact may be included and does 
not count against the two-page limit; 
5. References (no page limit) with citations supporting significant claims or reports of 
success; and 
6. Format specifications: 12-point Times New Roman font, single-sided, single-spaced, 8.5 × 
11-inch paper with 1-inch margins. 
 
Submission Instructions to Respondents 
Responses to this RFI are due no later than 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time, May 15, 2026. All submissions 
must be electronically submitted as PDF documents to dni-iarpa-rfi-26-01@iarpa.gov. Inquiries 
must be submitted to the same address. Do not send questions with proprietary content. No

Disclaimers and Important Notes 
This RFI is issued solely for information and planning purposes and does not constitute a

pay for information solicited, nor is it obligated to issue solicitations based on responses received. 
No proprietary and no classified concepts or information shall be included in 
submittals. Should respondents wish to submit classified information, prior coordination must be 
made with the IARPA Program Security Officer via email to the Primary Point of Contact. Input on

Audio Visual (AV) / Video Teleconferencing (VTC) Lifecycle Information Technology (IT) Support (AV LIT)

Hill Air Force Base 

Request for Information (RFI)

Overview 

The Air Force Nuclear Weapon Center (AFNWC) Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM) Systems Directorate (SD) team is conducting market research to define the scope and requirements of the Audio Visual (AV)/ Video Teleconferencing (VTC) Lifecycle Information Technology (IT) Support (AV LIT). For this RFI, Government is seeking input from industry on the capability to operate within a Special Access Program (SAP) environment. 

Scope

The primary objective of this contract is to provide lifecycle sustainment for current and future Traditional and Air Force Microsoft Teams (MS Teams) based Video Teleconferencing (VTC), Audio Visual (AV), and Information Technology (IT) hardware systems across ICBM Directorate Operating Locations in the Continental United States (CONUS). 

The Contractor shall provide comprehensive Consulting and Design Services for new and existing VTC and AV solutions, as well as for IT hardware installation. The Contractor shall also provide end-to-end Maintenance Services which include, but are not limited to, tier 3 support, decommissioning, and lifecycle replacement. 

To facilitate the procurement of necessary equipment and services, the Contractor shall follow the established Pricing Catalogue of pre-approved hardware, standard conference room hardware configurations, and associated services. Services and hardware may be requested in addition to the standardized configurations. This catalogue will be used for all purchasing and installation activities performed under this contract. Individual Task Orders may deviate from the Price Catalogue as negotiated between the requiring activity and the contractor. 

This contract requires the contractor to obtain and maintain necessary security clearances and to coordinate with ICBM personnel on all matters involving security impact and cybersecurity compliance, including the implementation and management of controls under the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIG) and Risk Management Framework (RMF). The contractor shall provide the organizational resources, both technical and functional, required for managing contract performance.

SOFTWARE METRICS
To deliver on its current and future mission, NGA needs to deliver useful software faster and more consistently. 
To measure progress toward this intent, NGA will track three key metrics for each software product: availability, lead time for 
changes, and deployment frequency. Additionally, each software product is expected to have its own product-specific metrics

The metrics and elements in this document, collectively referred to as “The NGA Software Way,” serve as an implementation guide

A NOTE FROM THE CTO 
To deliver on its current and future mission, NGA needs to deliver useful software faster 
and more consistently. To do this, the NGA Technology Strategy describes changes in 
approach, tools, and behavior that will result in faster iterations, more flexible products, 
and better-satisfied users and customers. The NGA Software Way is an implementation 
guide to supplement NGA’s Technology Strategy and provide additional specific 
guidance for teams building and operating software.
Our intent is to get to a place where NGA software products are designed and built 
with users, can be automatically updated in production daily, and use product-specific 
metrics to make decisions. We believe in small, empowered, cross-functional teams that 
deeply understand their users and constantly work directly with those users to deliver on 
their mission.
Implementing The NGA Software Way won’t happen all at once; we must start with 
iteratively tracking and improving these metrics and meeting each element below. As 
we do this together, and with an understanding of this intent, we will successfully deliver 
software products with the speed, accuracy, and precision NGA’s mission demands.   
SOFTWARE METRICS
The three initial metrics all programs must track for each software product delivered to users are availability, lead time for changes, 
and deployment frequency. It is important to note that NGA is not unique in using these metrics. These are three of the primary 
metrics DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) has studied over the past six years. These metrics use data from over 31,000 
professionals worldwide as well as rigorous statistical methods to study the most effective ways to develop and deploy technology. 
More information about the DORA metrics and study can be found in this DORA report: https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/
state-of-devops-2019.pdf.
These metrics provide visibility into how NGA balances speed (deployment frequency and lead time for changes) and stability 
(availability) during product development and operations. These two efforts, speed and stability, were once believed to be negatively 
correlated — increasing one would decrease the other. DORA research has conclusively shown that speed and stability are 
outcomes that enable each other and high-performing teams do better in both of these areas. This is what NGA is aiming for and 
moving toward. 
For software teams using NGA’s enterprise-managed version control and Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) 
pipeline, deployment frequency and lead time for changes will be automatically tracked within those services’ dashboards. To 
enable that automation, the recommended tagging method can be found in the appendix. For teams not using NGA’s enterprise-
managed version control and CI/CD pipeline, lead time for changes and deployment frequency must be independently calculated and 
transparently shared. All teams are expected to regularly share their metrics with teammates, stakeholders, users, and leadership. 
Eventually, teams will programmatically share these metrics to a central, NGA-managed location. 
AVAILABILITY
Availability is about ensuring a product or service is accessible to users when they need it. At a 
macro level, availability represents technology teams and organizations meeting user expectations 
about the software they are deploying and operating. Any time a user is not able to access a 
software product, that product is unavailable. Availability may be impacted by actions a product 
team itself takes or through issues with upstream or downstream dependencies. There is no 
distinction in availability to users based on what caused the issue; whether planned or unplanned 
and no matter where the issue originated, the impact of a product being unavailable when users 
need it is the same.
Alex Loehr
NGA Chief Technology Officer

PAGE |  3
Approved for Public Release, 22-195
Higher availability is better, as it means the product is accessible when users need and expect it. 
Tracking availability automatically enables teams to know when something goes wrong, giving the 
opportunity to investigate issues more rapidly and proactively. Although teams may have different 
availability requirements depending on mission and user needs, teams are generally expected to 
maintain at least 99.9% availability in production, which translates to about one business day of 
downtime per year.
LEAD TIME FOR CHANGES
Lead time for changes tracks how long it takes to deliver a feature for mission use once it has 
been developed. Lead time for changes is calculated as the median time between when code is 
committed to when it is deployed to a production environment, where it can be used during an 
actual mission (not in a test environment). That figure is measured across all commits within a 
given time period. Measuring this enables teams to understand where bottlenecks are in getting 
features to production and prioritize where to optimize. 
Shorter lead times are better because they enable faster feedback on what is built and allow 
teams to course correct more rapidly. Additionally, faster lead times allow faster fixes with higher 
confidence when there are issues, which directly impacts availability as well. DORA research 
shows high-performing teams have lead times for changes of less than one week. 
DEPLOYMENT FREQUENCY 
Deployment frequency is how often a product is deployed to production. A product team will 
do many additional deployments to testing, development, staging, and other non-production 
environments. The deployment frequency metric is specifically related to deployments to 
production, however, where users actually use the product to complete the mission or function. 
To the maximum extent possible, deployments are expected to be automated (see Automated 
Deployments on page 9), so increasing deployment frequency does not linearly increase workload 
on the team. 
Deployment frequency is a proxy for batch size. Reducing batch size has consistently been shown 
to accelerate feedback, improve efficiency, reduce risk and overhead, increase team motivation 
and urgency, and reduce costs (for more details, see Accelerate, page 16, by Nicole Forsgren, Jez 
Humble, and Gene Kim). DORA research shows high-performing teams deploy at least once per 
week.

products contribute to NGA’s mission in different ways, so their success must be uniquely measured, 
and each team must define its own product-specific metrics.

1 | REPTILE RFI 
Solicitation Number: USSOCOM RFI REPTILE (Rapid Experimentation of 
Prototyping Technology in Learning Environments): Counter-Unmanned-Systems (C-
UxS)  
Notice Type: Special Notice 
TYPE: A–Research and Development 
NAICS: 541715 Research and Development in the Physical, Engineering, and Life 
Sciences (except Nanotechnology and Biotechnology) 
Publish Date: April 07, 2026 
Response Date: April 21, 2026, 12:00 Noon Eastern Daylight Time (EDT)  
 
A.  INTRODUCTION: REPTILE (Rapid Experimentation of Prototyping Technology 
in Learning Environments)    
This Request for Information (RFI) is NOT a solicitation for proposals, proposal 
abstracts, or quotations. The purpose of this RFI is to solicit technology experimentation 
candidates from Research and Development (R&D) organizations, private industry, and 
academia for inclusion in future experimentation events coordinated by the U. S. 
Special Operations Command (USSOCOM). USSOCOM invites industry, academia, 
individuals, and Government labs to submit technology experimentation nominations 
addressing innovative technologies identified in paragraph 4 below. The intent is to 
provide participants with the opportunity to gain Special Operations Forces (SOF) 
insight/perspective on participant technologies. 
The REPTILE event will explore emerging technologies, technical applications, and their 
potential to provide solutions for future SOF capabilities. This RFI is for REPTILE 26. 
This event will occur over the period of one week.    
Dates/Theme/Location:   
June 2026: Counter-Unmanned-Systems (C-UxS) – Gulfport, MS. 
B.  OBJECTIVE:  
1. The REPTILE event provides an opportunity for technology developers to operate 
and have their technology assessed by operational personnel through environmental 
scenarios to determine how their technology development efforts and ideas may 

UNCLASSIFIED   
UNCLASSIFIED  
2 | REPTILE RFI 
support or enhance SOF capability needs. The environment facilitates a 
collaborative relationship between Government, academia, and industry to promote 
the identification and assessment of emerging technologies. 
2. The deadline for nomination package(s) is April 21, 2026, at 12:00 Noon EDT. After 
reviewing the nomination submissions, the Government may invite select candidates 
to demonstrate their technologies at the USSOCOM sponsored REPTILE 2026 
event. Experiments will be conducted during June 2026, Gulf Coast area, and will 
explore emerging technology solutions and revolutionary improvements in relevant 
technologies. Preference will be given to materiel solutions between a Technology 
Readiness Level (TRL) of 6 and above. There is no intention on the part of 
USSOCOM to purchase or procure equipment based solely on participation in 
REPTILE 2026. 
3. Experimentation Focus: The primary intent of this event is to highlight technologies 
that support C-UxS and friendly advanced Unmanned Systems (UxS) operations. 
Experiments will be conducted in unimproved expeditionary-like conditions with a 
dismounted special operations team. Relevant networks and an Android Tactical 
Assault Kit (ATAK) capability will be available at the event for integration and/or 
operations with participating experiments. Depending on the technology selection 
some integration and/or collaboration with existing SOF technology may be an 
opportunity. 
4. Experimentation Problem Statement: Special Operators have a need to defeat a 
swarm of up to 100x, Group 1-2, autonomous drones while operating in a denied 
areas from a static position within wooded terrain in day and night conditions. 
5. Design Reference Mission: A special operations team infiltrated behind enemy 
lines to conduct a 5-day special reconnaissance mission. The team established a 
Mission Support Site and Observation Point in wooded terrain observing and 
reporting on an enemy facility. The team emplaced detection technologies and set 
up defensive measures to counter drone swam threats. After 48 hours, the team 
identified indications, warnings and their position was compromised and the enemy 
was sending a drone swarm to find, fix, and finish the team. The team’s detection 
equipment identified the threat and relayed it to the team and its defensive effectors. 
The effectors engaged with and destroyed the threat, allowing the team to 
successfully exfil without any casualties. 

UNCLASSIFIED   
UNCLASSIFIED  
3 | REPTILE RFI 
6. Technology areas to explore during the event include the following: 
6.1. Counter-Unmanned Systems (C-UxS) Technologies: USSOCOM is seeking 
C-UxS technologies that can quickly detect, track, identify, classify, and 
neutralize individual Unmanned Systems (UxS) and swarms of UxS. 
Technologies will operate in multi-domains including ground, air, maritime and at 
times may traverse multiple in one operation. Key areas of interest include: 
6.1.1. Integrated detection and engagement capabilities. 
6.1.2 Early warning systems. 
6.1.3 Semi-autonomous and autonomous platforms. 
6.1.4 Integration into existing C2 systems. 
6.1.5 Electromagnetic (EM) hardened systems. 
6.1.6 Low Collateral Effectors: Precision non-kinetic and kinetic solutions for use 
in complex environments. 
6.1.7 Electromagnetic protection (EP) systems that can detect, characterize, and 
geolocate electromagnetic interference (EMI). 
6.1.8. EMI detection finding (direction, target location- within 40m). 
6.2. Modular, Low SWaP- CUxS & Rapidly Produced (All UxS Types): 
6.2.1.  Modular components, multi-factor components and integrations. 
6.2.2.  Low-cost/attritable/disposable/rapidly produced CUxS effectors. 
6.2.3. Software-agnostic. 
6.2.4. Kinetic/non-kinetic and or mixed modular payloads. 
6.2.5. Edge UxS production and maintenance. 
6.2.6. Tactical UxS weaponry. 
6.2.7. Low SWaP jam-resistant GPS antennas or other operational PNT 
solutions. 
6.3. Counter-UxS Capability Focus: 
6.3.1. Operator-worn/portable UxS detection/localization/classification 
(Passive). 
6.3.2. Novel defeat capabilities (portable, UxS-mounted, vehicle-mounted 
low SWaP).  
6.3.3. Low-SWaP kinetic defeat (not ammunition specifically) 
6.3.4. Low-collateral kinetic  
6.3.5.  Omni-detection coverage.

6.3.6. Allows short-to-medium term stationary deployment and/or mobile 
options for tactical teams. 
6.3.7.  RF Based cyber takeover technology. 
6.3.8. Provides end-to-end detection and mitigation for situational 
awareness and operational continuity. 
6.4. Unmanned and Autonomous Systems (UAS/UxS) Technologies. We are 
seeking the best Group 1-2 UAS technologies that can operate despite of 
adversarial C-UxS technologies. Desired capabilities include: 
6.4.1. EM Hardening: Robust C2 links and GPS/GNSS receivers. 
6.4.2. Swarming/Collaborative Autonomy: Multiple UxS operating as a 
cohesive unit to survive threats. 
6.4.3. Tethered Systems (with mobility). 
6.4.4. Enhanced Survivability: Low-observable characteristics and onboard 
threat detection. 
6.4.5. Multi-purpose, multi-domain technologies and/or systems. 
6.4.6. Deployable from undersea. 
6.4.7. Rapid deployment to underwater location.  
6.4.8. Vertical integration.  
6.4.8.1. Ability to deliver payloads to undersea locations. 
6.4.9. Payload retrieval from undersea. 
6.4.10. Waterproof, robust, weatherproof platform. 
6.4.11. Fast transition from air to sea, or sea to air. 
6.5. Unmanned Systems (UxS) - All Domains 
6.5.1. Multi-Modal, Multi-Domain Capabilities: 
6.5.1.1. Single systems (air, land, sea, space). 
6.5.1.2. Low-cost, attritable sensors/payloads w/ volatile firmware & 
remote zeroizing (SIGINT, EW, IMINT, GEOINT, ELINT, 
MASINT), including RF deception/decoy payloads. 
6.5.1.3. Low SWaP phased antenna arrays. 
6.5.1.4.  Multi-modal, cognitive, intelligent communication systems 
6.5.1.5. Biomimicry. Modeled after living organisms. 
6.5.1.6. Multi-domain Automatic Threat/Target Recognition (ATR) 
algorithms (agnostic datasets). 
6.5.1.7. No-code/low-code multi-domain edge ATR training.

Proposed solutions that include components enhancing resilience and survivability 
of SOF teams in Counter UxS operations may include the following components 
and/or technologies intended to be evaluated or assessed.

6.6.1.  UxS common controllers/architectures. 
6.6.2.  Inter-agent communications. 
6.6.3. AI-enabled swarming algorithms. 
6.6.4. Multi-domain delivery/charging platforms. 
6.6.5. Manned/unmanned teaming with collaborative alerts for situational 
awareness. 
6.7. UxS Human-Machine Interface (HMI) & AI/Sensor Integration: 
6.7.1. AI for autonomy. 
6.7.2. Novel RF/non-RF control architectures. 
6.7.3. Multi-modal UxS control (single/multi-agent, End User Device-based). 
6.7.4. Bi-directional state sharing. 
6.7.5. Advanced UxS/AR displays. 
6.7.6. Hands-free command. 
6.7.7. AI-enabled COP. 
6.7.8. Multi-sensor fusion. 
6.7.9. ATR integration. 
6.7.10. Commercial Internet of Things integration. 
6.8. Blue Force Awareness Technology: 
6.8.1. Devices/tech to distinguish friend/foe on UxS platforms visually/digitally. 
6.8.2. Lightweight Air Launched Effects Delivery System. 
6.8.3. Lightweight, precision, glide systems. 
6.8.4. GPS-denied navigation. 
6.8.5. Semi-active laser designator. 
6.8.6. Payload <10lbs, overall system <30lbs. 
7. Security/Classification Requirements: Respondents shall not submit classified 
information in the technology experimentation nominations. If respondents believe 
classified information is required for their proposal please contact 
tech_exp@socom.mil to coordinate appropriate information.

PERFORMANCE WORK STATEMENT FOR 
DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS CAPITAL INVESTMENT OPTIONS 

FY2028 / FY2029 CAPITAL BUDGET DOCUMENTS  

GENERAL INFORMATION

Title of Project: Capital Investment Options IDIQ - FY2028 / FY2029 Capital Budget Documents Task Order 

Scope of Work: The contractor shall provide all resources necessary to accomplish the types of deliverables described in this Performance Work Statement (PWS) to assist the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) in the preparation of Capital Budget Documents to inform the FY2028 President’s Budget Request and FY2029 Budget Request, if needed. Major Construction projects and Major and Mid-Level Leases anticipated for the Strategic Capital Investment Planning (SCIP) 2028 and 2029 cycles will have been identified and will be scored using the SCIP Decision Criteria Model, resulting in a prioritized list of projects developed through the VA governance process for inclusion in VA’s FY2028 Budget Submission. As part of VA’s submission to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), an OMB300 Application and associated documents will be prepared for all Major Construction projects and Prospectuses and associated documents for Major and Mid-Level Leases.

This contract ensures VA’s ability to replace healthcare facilities that are significantly deficient in seismic compliance, infrastructure, or space through the authorization and approval by Congress of approved Major Construction projects and Major Leases. Without timely delivery of OMB300 Applications and supporting documentation, VHA’s strategic capital priority projects would fail to receive funding, approvals, or required authorizations. The services under this contract directly support the delivery of modern, safe, and accessible infrastructure that meets the evolving needs of Veterans—particularly underserved, rural, and women Veterans—ensuring that VA’s capital investments translate into improved access, reduced service gaps, and enhanced quality of care.

This contract builds upon more than a decade of programmatic support under similar scopes, benefiting from institutional knowledge, toolsets, and contractor familiarity with VA’s capital investment process. Maintaining continuity is essential for efficient onboarding, stakeholder coordination, and meeting complex statutory and regulatory submission requirements.

The FY2028 / FY2029 Capital Budget Documents contract is not merely a technical support mechanism, it is a mission-critical strategic tool that underpins the execution of VA’s capital investment portfolio. Managed by Office of Construction and Facilities Management’s (CFM) Office of Real Property (ORP), this contract enables the development and submission of Non-IT Business Case Applications essential to executing congressionally approved Major Construction projects and Prospectus packages for Major Leases as required by U.S.C. § 8104 and Title 40 U.S.C. § 3301 et seq., while also ensuring alignment with OMB Circular A-11, Appendix B. These statutory frameworks and guidance govern how VA submits Major Construction projects and Major Leases for Congressional approval, and manages, and scores real property lease obligations, with direct implications for Veteran’s access to modern, safe, and effective medical facilities.

In accordance with the Bona-Fide Needs Rule (31 U.S.C. § 1502(a)), this contract addresses an immediate and legitimate need of the VA to support the development of a well-structured and justified Budget Requests for Major Construction Projects and Leases that will enhance facilities and services for Veterans. The services provided under this contract are essential to ensuring that VA funding requests align with VA’s strategic priorities, comply with federal budgeting and procurement laws, and optimize the allocation of taxpayer dollars. By conducting rigorous assessments and preparing detailed Non-IT Business Case Applications, this effort directly supports the VA’s mission to improve healthcare, benefits, and services for Veterans, as mandated under 38 U.S.C. § 7301 (Functions of the Veterans Health Administration) and the VA Major Construction and Lease Authorization Act.

Background: The SCIP process is the basis for VA’s current and out-year capital budget requests. The SCIP process includes development of 10-Year Action Plans and budget year Business Cases to close performance gaps (space, utilization, facility condition, etc.) to enhance healthcare and delivery of services and benefits for the nation’s Veterans.

In the late 1990s, VA began a dramatic change in the way it delivers services, shifting from an in-patient, hospital-based model to one that focuses on preventive care in outpatient settings. That shift has left VA with an increasing inventory of aging and obsolete facilities, many in locations where there is diminished demand. To build upon past capital planning efforts, and to address the problem of aging infrastructure in poor condition, lack of infrastructure in some locations and unused infrastructure in others, the Department has embarked on the SCIP process. SCIP is a significant and critical initiative that will enable VA to better adapt to changes in the environment, demographics, capabilities, medical technology, and health care delivery, thereby allowing VA to deliver the highest quality healthcare, benefits, and memorial services to our Nation’s veterans.

SCIP ensures that all resources will be scrutinized and considered at the corporate level, with equitable and consistent distribution across markets and competing capital needs to address gaps in our service delivery. SCIP provides the Secretary with a project list that is integrated across all administrations and programs (Major and Minor Construction, Leases, and Non- Recurring Maintenance) to ensure resources are allocated to address the most critical gaps.

With the strategic goal to improve the delivery of services and benefits to Veterans, the SCIP process will be the basis for the Department’s FY2028 Capital Budget Request. Unlike previous capital planning models, SCIP links planning efforts of the Administrations and Staff Offices for both capital and non-capital solutions and takes a long-term departmental approach. SCIP also encourages investments that ensure delivery of services in a Veteran-centric, forward-looking, and results-driven manner, while placing particular emphasis on improving access, maintaining our capital portfolio, increasing market penetration, reducing homelessness, and ameliorating issues confronting women Veterans.

Currently, VA has a significant funding backlog in construction projects and Facility Condition Assessment deficiencies, and many of its facilities are over-utilized, resulting in higher maintenance costs and inefficient resource usage.

Closing critical identified gaps will be the basis for FY2028 SCIP Business Case applications developed by the Administrations and Staff Offices. Business Cases will be prepared for Major Construction, Minor Construction, Major Leases, and Mid-Level Leases, since these are more complex and represent a higher risk to VA.

The Business Cases will be scored using the SCIP Decision Criteria Model resulting in a prioritized list of projects through VA’s governance process for inclusion in the FY2028 or FY2029 Budget Request. This scope of work is to assist VA with the preparation of Non-IT Business Case Applications for Major Construction projects and Prospectus and Budget Documents for Major and Mid-Level Leases for inclusion in VA’s FY2028 and FY2029 President’s Budget Requests.

 

Performance Period: The period of performance is for 365 calendar days from date of award. Work at the Government site shall not take place on Federal holidays or weekends unless directed by the Contracting Officer (CO).

Type of Contract: Firm Fixed Price task order.

Place of Performance: The primary place of performance will be at the contractor’s facilities; however, some tasks may require work to be performed at a Government facility. Any work at the Government site shall not take place on Federal holidays or weekends, unless directed by the CO.

CONTRACT AWARD MEETING

The contractor shall not commence performance on the tasks in this PWS until the CO has conducted a kick-off meeting or has advised the contractor that a kick-off meeting is waived.

GENERAL REQUIREMENTS

The following general requirements apply to this task order:

Unless otherwise specified in an individual task, the following schedule requirements apply: Where a written milestone deliverable is required in draft form, the VA will complete their review of the draft deliverable within five calendar days from date of receipt. The contractor shall have seven calendar days to deliver the final deliverable from date of receipt of the Government’s comments.

The contractor shall provide to the Contracting Officer’s Representative (COR), via email, documentation related to all government-contractor meetings. The contractor shall provide this documentation within one calendar day after completion of the meeting unless otherwise specified in an individual task.

Except for proprietary information in company quotes identified and marked in accordance with FAR 52.215-1(e), the contractor shall not deliver to CFM any proprietary products or information of any type in completing the requirements of each task under this PWS. The contractor’s internal development tools (that is, those development tools not developed for CFM work and not required by CFM to install, use, or revise the deliverables) are exempted from this requirement. If the contractor believes an exception to this requirement is necessary for the effective or efficient execution of a task, the contractor shall request a specific exception, in writing, to the CO, and shall not use the proprietary tools or information in CFM work until approval is received from the CO.

The contractor shall ensure contract employees maintain an open and professional communication with the staff at all VA facilities. For transparency purposes, email to the CO shall not be blind carbon copied (BCC) to other Government personnel. Complaints or violation validated by the COR or VA staff will be reported in writing to the CO, Office of Inspector General (OIG), or Head of Contracting Activities (HCA) for action. If the contractor fails to correct validated complaints raised by the COR and or CO, it will be considered a failure in performance.

The CO may require the contractor to meet with the COR, contract administrator, and/ or other Government personnel at least quarterly, and as often as deemed necessary. The contractor may request a meeting with the CO when deemed necessary.

SPECIFIC MANDATORY TASKS AND ASSOCIATED DELIVERABLES

Description of Tasks and Associated Deliverables: The contractor shall provide the specific deliverables described below within the performance period stated in Section A.4 of this PWS.

Task One: PMP and Briefing

The contractor shall provide a Performance Management Plan (PMP) and briefing for the project team, which presents the contractor's plan for completing the task order. The contractor's plan shall be responsive to this PWS and describe, in further detail, the approach to be used for each aspect of the task as defined in the technical proposal. The contractor shall keep the PMP up to date throughout the period of performance. 

Deliverable 1: PMP and Briefing

Task Two: Communications

2.1 Kick-off Meeting

2.2 Status Teleconferences (weekly)

Deliverable 2: Kick-Off Meeting and up to fifty-two weekly Status Teleconferences with all related documentation distributed prior to call and after each call. 

Task Three: Prospectus and Non-IT OMB300 Business Case Packages – Major Construction (Up to 10- Approved Projects)

Non-IT Business Case Forms & Attachments

Provide services, information, and data as necessary to assist VA in the preparation of budget documentation, Non-IT OMB300 Business Cases (also known as OMB Exhibit 300 Forms), for the designated projects.

Prepare responses (with assistance from appropriate Veterans Integrated Service Network (VISN)/ VA Medical Center (VAMC) staff) to all Non-IT OMB300 Business Case Form questions.

Conduct site searches to confirm availability of vacant land in given markets and determine average land costs for lease alternatives.

Perform high level real estate market studies to determine average rent and operating/maintenance costs for use in lease alternatives.

Work with CFM to validate project scope and cost and obtain latest cost estimates. This includes comparison of current project scope to the previously approved project baseline, with any project scope or project size discrepancy being fully documented.

Conduct Cost Effectiveness Analyses (CEAs). VA will provide the CEA template to ensure use of the latest SCIP guidance.

Perform Risk Analyses. Attachment A provides a sample of the expected Risk Analysis deliverable.

BACKGROUND

The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Chief Information Officer (CIO) organization – through its Office of Information and Technology (OIT) – is responsible for integrating, securing, and modernizing the information technology that underpins VA’s delivery of care, benefits, and services to millions of Veterans. VA OIT currently staffs roughly 8,000 IT professionals, with budget authority of approximately $7.3 billion for IT systems in FY 2026. This includes significant investments in enterprise modernization programs such as Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM), Financial Management Business Transformation (FMBT), and other major enterprise solutions, while also addressing cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, and legacy system retirement. 

As VA pursues these complex, multi-year IT transformations against a backdrop of workforce reorganization, reductions in staffing levels, and evolving technology demands, there is a clear need for structured, data-driven workforce gap analysis to inform strategic planning, risk management, and investment decisions that will help ensure mission success and continuity of services for Veterans. Specifically, VA OIT should consider acting on the following critical activities to ensure VA OIT’s ability to meet the urgent needs of current service delivery and plan for the future: 

Identify the future needs of the OIT workforce 

Identify skill areas that are lacking in OIT

Develop solutions to support workforce improvement initiatives 

Identify needs for future hiring

Below sections outline the comprehensive, multi-phase strategy required to identify and address workforce gaps for VA OIT. 

APPLICABLE DOCUMENTS

VA Directive 0710, “Personnel Security and Suitability Program,” June 4, 2010, https://www.va.gov/vapubs/index.cfm
